Yeah, I think there is. It's slightly complicated though and some people might protest it.

Think of the front page or /all/ as a pie. You allocate "slices" (percentages) of space on them to subverses.

This is the easy way (an example):

25 links/page, so 20% space for /v/news, 20% space for /v/politics, 20% space for /v/technology, 20% for /v/books.

That means 5 links per subverse on the front page. The result is that you will always have 5 links from /v/news no matter what. These links would be the top 5 /v/news submissions (as seen in "Hot" of /v/news.)

This is the more complicated, but better way:

You set a max number of links allowed per subverse instead. You use the percentage allocation again, but instead of fixing it at 20% (or whatever percentage, 20% was just an example, 5 to 10% is more realistic to include as many subverses as possible, lets use x%) you set the max number of links allowed per subverse at x%. This stops /v/news from dominating the front page (and/or /all/) as it can no longer take up more than (lets just say) 10% of the front page but doesn't necessarily have to use up it's 10%.

What this does is make it so that something from /v/books isn't competing directly with all the /v/news submissions, but doesn't make it mandatory that /v/books be on the front page if it isn't popular enough.

Also, it should extend over to page 5 or so, because it would be unseemly and weird if the 1st page was like that and then you suddenly got a flood of submissions from one subverse the moment you click on the next page.

Areas for further thought: should the percentage allocations be equal? Should some subverses (deemed more important) be given more space?

Anyways, this will address the "equitable discussion" issue that MarkW has brought up (an important one,) as well as another problem that someone else (don't remember name) mentioned with gifs and pics covering up the front page of reddit.
